blocks.x: Okay. Good evening. This is Lawrence Marrero. I'm 58 years old. Born October 28, 1900.

You can just lean back or you don't have to lean back. Just relax. The date was October? The 24th of October. I made a mistake. October 24th. Yeah. 1900. What part of town were you, where were you raised? Where were you born? Remember the house or the street?
Well, I was born down in 7 Ward, around Mendeville Street. And the bill and what else? Around Mendeville and Prea down that way.
Your father, of course, was a well-known musician, Billy Marrero. What was his full name? Do you know?
Yeah, Bill. My father is named William Marrero.
Everybody called him Billy. Everybody called him Billy for short. Do you have a middle name, do you remember?
Well, no. I thought they called him Billy.
Can you remember about how old he was and when he died?
My father was 47 when he died, Bill.
47? Yeah. Which wasn't very old.
No. Well, he died around 1917.
Did you ever hear him play bass much?

Oh, yeah, Bill. Yeah. I used to follow my dad a lot. I heard that when he was ten years old, I remember, when he had the band with Bump and Peter Bocall and Violet and Richard Payne. And Walter Brunley, I think the drum player was named. Buddy Johnson's trombone.
Yeah.
And the ghetto player was Richard. Richard, I forget his last name, but anyhow.
Is that Payne? Richard Payne. Richard Payne. That's right. Richard Payne. That's right. Yeah. Who was the clarinet, do you remember?
Yeah, Big Eye Louie. Big Eye Louie. Yeah, Louie Nelson.
What was the name of that band?
That was the Imperial.
Is it Imperial? You sure? Yeah. Or was it Superior, maybe? Yeah, yeah.
I think it was Imperial or Superior, one of those bands. I just remember quite the name, but Imperial or Superior, one of those names.
And your father, I guess, was manager, said that on his cap and that picture.
Well, he was manager of the band, yeah, but we didn't have such thing as leader then, it was manager then. Yeah.
Where did you live in those days? In the same neighborhood, or had you moved?
Well, no, Bill. I lived in around 1200 block, two row, that's between Murray and Oich Court.
Mm-hmm.
That's around 1910.

Since your father, of course, was never interviewed by anybody, I suppose, since they began writing about jazz, I was interested if you could find just a few facts about him. Did he ever play anything except bass, do you know?
Well, yeah. He was a guitar player too, played guitar too.
You know which one he started on? Bass violin. He started on bass violin. That was his main instrument.
That's his main instrument, bass violin. But he played guitar. He played guitar too, yeah. Anything else? Well, no, that's all I remember. My father played guitar and bass violin.
Do you remember, was he a pretty good reader? That is, did he usually read music?
No, my father never was a reading musician. He never read a music.
He wasn't a reading musician. I thought maybe he was. No. No, he never did.
No.
Did he, who was your first teacher? Your teacher?
My first teacher to my brother, John Marrero.
Oh, your father didn't teach you then? No, my father didn't teach me. John taught me. Do you remember any other bands that your father ever told that he played in?

Well, Bill, he did tell me many bands he played in. Tell the truth, I don't know whether it was Emmanuel Perez or Joe Oliver. I know he played with Freddie Keppel. He did, he was a man. He did have Freddie Keppel with him. With him and his band. Yeah, his band, yes. And he had another trumpet player. We used to call him a cornet player. That was named Nene Kwaku. Oh, yeah. That was a trumpet player. I heard it. But one time.
Did anyone else in your family, that is, were there any uncles, the older members, your mother play anything or did she sing?
Oh, yes, Bill. My mother used to sing and she was a good, good guitar player.
Your mother was a guitar player?

My mother gave me a lot of chords on guitars. Oh, really? Yeah, she really was a good guitar player. Yeah, she really was a good guitar player. Mm-hmm. The fact about it, Bill, we all used to get in the kitchen or the bedroom, my two brothers, my father and my mother, and get to get all string instruments and play. Oh, my. And I remember this is good, playing guitar then. The first number I was, they learned me was under the double eagle. So many changes, it was really good too, to hear all them string instruments play them together. It really was good.
But your brother John is the one that taught you? Yeah, my brother John. Did he just teach you by ear at first or did he try to teach you to read by the way? Well, no, he teach me by ear.

Mm-hmm. He teach me by ear. That's how I learned first. But I learned music long, long years after when I put up my own band with Bush Hall's name, Paul Barnes, my brother, Edward Moreira, bass violin, and my cousin Josiah Frazier on drums.
Oh, while we're talking about that, how are you related to Paul Barnes and Emil Barnes, of course. They're cousins too, aren't they?
Well, I'm the first cousin Bill. Well, uh.
How is that family related now? If you can explain a little bit. Well, yes Bill.

The Frazier's too. Yeah, I can explain you that. Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes' mother and my mother, two sisters. What was your mother's maiden name then? My mother's maiden name was, her maiden name was Frazier, Jeanette Frazier. Now, uh, the Frazier's, Josiah Frazier's name, their father and my mother were citizen brothers. Yeah, I see. Yeah.
So Saiz, your first cousin. First cousin.
Emile Barnes and Paul Barnes, also my first cousin.

Um, let's see if I can think of anything else, or if you can think of anything else really, about your father. Um, I don't suppose you ever played anything in, uh, brass bands, any, some of those fellows that play like bass drum or something in a brass band like you did, you know?
Well, uh, Bill, uh, my brother Simon, he was a bass drum player and also a sousaphone player
in brass band.
Oh, Simon. Yeah, Simon, he plays, how do you call it, Pelican, Helican?
Yeah, Pelican.
Yeah, he did play that in brass band and, uh, he also played bass drum. That's why I took it up behind him.
You don't remember your father ever playing bass drum? No, no, no, my dad played bass drum, never did, no Bill.
Nothing. He might have played, but I never remember him playing no bass drum.
Did any of your uncles or aunts play anything too, and the members of the Frazier family?

Yes, Bill, I had an uncle, he was a piano tuner. Well then he played bass violin also, Michelle Frazier. Piano tuner? He's a piano tuner and he rappelled. Yeah. And his son, he had a son called Mitchell Frazier, was a great piano player. Not musical, just head, you know?
Yeah, just good talent, sorry. Yeah. Um, can you tell some more now about your brothers, uh, since some of them are dead? How many brothers altogether did you have?
Bill, uh, we was five brothers and two sisters. Now, we're three of us living now. Since my brother Simon and John is dead, well that make me be the oldest one living. Oldest one.
How much older were they than you now? Was John, uh, or Simon oldest?

Well Simon was the oldest. John was next and I come right behind John. Then Eddie is behind me, also a good musician, was a good musician. I reckon you have heard him play baseball already. Yeah, I do. Yeah, he was really good too. He stopped playing. Oh, okay.

We were talking about your brothers. Um, Simon was the, uh... Oldest. Oldest. And then John. And then Lauren. Uh, how much older was John than you? Do you remember about? Well, uh, John was about three years older than me. Just about three years. Yeah. And, uh, when did he die? Was that in New York did he die? Well, yeah, he died in New York, Bill. I remember if he died if he died I got killed by now.
It was in New York when he passed.
Okay, was that in New York that he died?
Well yeah, he died in New York, Bill. I remember the day he died, if he died, I got killed by now. He was in New York when he passed. We didn't know until a day or so after.
Was that about 1940 or so? I knew he was up there.
Something like that, Bill, around 40 or 41, something like that, yeah.

Can you remember some of the bands he played in? About the only one we can always hear about is the Celestan Band, but do you remember anything about his life at all that he ever told you or that you can remember when you were a little baby, practically, he must have been playing when you were pretty young.

Well, Bill, I do remember him, he played with Sam Morgan's band. I remember that good, and Buddy Petit Band also. Simon and Joan was a member of the Buddy Petit Band, jazz band, and it was also myself I played with Buddy Petit.
We'll talk about that in a minute there.

Yeah, I was off with him in Pensacola, Florida for quite a while. Then I also, I wasn't a member with the Sam Morgan Band, but I did go on a trip with him because his bandit player was Waken and couldn't get off. Was that Davis? That Johnny Dave. Dave. Johnny Dave, yeah. And I made a lot of trouble with the Sam Morgan Band, and I was a regular member of the Chris Kelly jazz band. Myself, my brother, Eddie, and my cousin, Emil Bones. We was a member of the Chris Kelly band. We had a wonderful jazz band.
Was Kid Howard in it at that time? No, Kid Howard, no. He meant later when he was a drummer.
Yeah, we see, Kid Howard first started on, was a drummer.
Yeah. Yeah.
But that time Kid Howard wasn't playing no music.
Yeah. To get back to John, can you remember, you say he's the first one that taught you. John the first one taught you. Did he play anything except banjo? Did he play guitar?
Oh yeah, he's a wonderful ghetto player.
Did he ever learn any other instrument?

Well, tomorrow, remember, that's all John did to play ghetto. That time we had six strings banjo, which he was then. Oh yeah. Yeah, you remember that six strings banjo. Well, he played a lot of piano too.
Well, he did. Yeah, he played good. He's a nice piano player.
Also, his wife, his wife is a great musician. She also now plays churches. Is she still living? Yeah, she's still living.
Well, we must get her address sometime. We'll talk to her. Maybe she remembers some. He probably told her.
Well, I'll tell you, Bill, whenever you get ready, I'll talk to her and bring her up here and let you.
Or we could go to her home sometime.
Yeah, well, that'd be nice. She'd be glad to do that. Because she could give you a lot of talk about John.
Do you remember anything about the other bands he played in? Or when he started, who his teacher was? Or anything about it? If he picked it up himself?
No, I think John picked it up himself. All under my father.
Yeah, just to be honest.

Yeah, just to be honest. Yeah, just to be honest. My father kind of give all his ideas. Yeah, same family. I don't know why. So they claim my father was a first-class bass violin player. I know they had not a lot of other good bass violin players. But just to say my father was one of the best.
Yeah, I'm sure. That's what everybody says, yeah.
Yeah, one of the best routines. Both of them, my brother Simon and my father.
Maybe you can tell us a little bit about Simon. How did he play anything else besides bass? Oh yeah, he was a sousaphone player. Oh, did he play in brass bands or anything? Yeah.
He was, then he played with a drum player, bass drum player like myself.
Oh yeah. Yeah, he was pretty good. I suppose you know who he learned from? Mostly your father I guess and around the family.
Most of my father taught them, taught all of us how to handle our instruments.
When they were young, did they all play your father's bass? Did they get instruments right away or what?

No, they didn't get them. They all, we all learned on one of the instruments. Uh-huh. See? And I did pick up sousaphone one time, but it was a little difficult for me so I wouldn't bother with it anymore. But the bass, I also did pick up the bass. I used to play bass. Yeah, I was in the first class bass, but I could play.
Yeah.
But my brother, he continued on and he made a good bass player.
Do you remember the very first instrument you got? Was it the guitar or banjo? It was a guitar. It was a guitar.
It was a guitar. Six string, was it?
Six string guitar. Six string. Yeah. And your brother then showed you some of the cards and the- He showed me all the cards of the 100.

Yeah, Bill Nath. If he wouldn't have died so early, I'd have been better off than I am today. I'd have been a more better musician. Because what the music I know and what he would teach me, that would give me a lot of advancements, Bill.

Hold on. Yeah, one second. I wanted to ask Lawrence, how do you spell your name? I've seen people spell it L-A-U. I think that's a French or Italian way of spelling Lawrence. How is it spelled for sure?
Bill, my name is spelled L-A-W-R-E-N-C-E.
Yeah, and the last name is-
It's M-A-R-R-E-R-O.
Yes, the two R's together. Lawrence Marrero. Three R's all together.
But now, Bill, I have a middle name.
Oh, yes.
What's the middle name? I don't use that middle name. It's Henry. Henry. It's H. Lawrence H. Marrero. Yeah, but I very seldom use that middle name.

Yeah. Now to get back, oh, another question. This town over here, Marrero, was that named- Do you know if your folks might have come way back from- I think that was named after the sheriff of some- Well, Bill, that's something- You know anything about way back?
Yeah, something I've heard, Bill, but I wouldn't say anything about that name to my father, you know?
Yeah.
because it may cause something, but I heard how my daddy got that name

and I'll just go by that way. I just wonder if it's from the family way back in the colonial times probably. To get on with your musical education, we'll say, when you started on banjo, your brother used to help you. Oh yes. Did you play in a band pretty quick then?

Yeah, yes indeed. I played a band pretty quick. I remember my brother John sent me in his place. He was with Sam Morgan one time ago, he sent me with Sam Morgan and Kid Ora was on trombone. We was advertised in the street then, in trucks. I remember that this guy played in his place and many jobs I played in the Papa Salastain Band in my brother John's place.
Do you remember your very first job? Was that the one you substituted in Morgan's band?

No, that's not my first job, Bill. I had a lot of, when I got, I made my own band, I had a lot of jobs of my own. See, after I made up my band and got around playing little house parties and going on, I got bigger jobs. Well how old were you when you first? I was 17 years old, Bill, when I started playing.
You must have started on something before then with that musical family, didn't you?
Well Bill, I would start with my instrument. Yeah. But banjo, six string banjo.
That was tuned like a guitar then.
That's right, yes.
When you first started on your brother started helping you, were you 17 then or younger than that? Oh, younger than that Bill.
That's what I thought. Yeah, I was playing at 17. Oh yeah. Yeah, I was playing at 17. Making money, playing jobs.
That's right. Um, had you ever played any other little homemade instruments or ever blow on little flute or anything when you followed parades or?
No Bill, all my instrument was, was ghetto, banjo and drum and baseball and outside instruments I never fooled.
You never fooled making a drum set of your own
or beating on anything or anything like that? No, I never did do that Bill. Like I told you, I did try a sousa form but it was too difficult for me and I'll put it down. I'll unfold that. Yep.
Uh, what was the first music you ever heard? Can you remember? It would be around home no doubt. Yes Bill. Did your father ever practice at home or?
Oh yes, yes and yeah. Bill they practiced at home most ever did. Also John and Sensei used to come home.
When your father would practice, did he practice sometime by himself on new pieces or was it usually somebody else came in and played with him?
Well he always practiced by himself on different things called. He always was a good chord man and a good bull man on bass.
Oh that's what I wanted to ask too. Did he play mostly bow or kicking in those ways?

Mostly bow. You could hear him anywhere. See sometime at night he'd have such a fairground and you could hear the beat just as good lead hours at night. You could hear the beat just as good humming. He really was a, not to brag cause he's my father. I know everybody says you don't have to be. Bill he was really good. It's different now than it was that time. And like I said Bill, I sat down and listened to a different band and we had some wonderful bands. But they're not playing the stuff that my dad and him used to play. I believe that. We just, we, my, uh, count myself too. We just trying to do what they used to do. And that's the truth. I'm not gonna lie about that. Like some fella says we do this and we do that. We don't do nothing. We trying to do.
Some people talk like everything is improving all the time. That things are getting better.
No Bill. It's getting more, it's going back for the, for the music playing. Before that time Bill, we used to play really understanding music.
Do you think they were better musicians, more talented to start with? Or did they just work harder at their instrument? Or did they take more pains and more interest? Yeah.

What was it do you think? They take more pains and more interest. In their wake. It seems they love their music more. Because the, the, the boys they there, they just jump up and if they can play one or two numbers, they're gone. They think they're professional.
They think they're professional. Those days I guess they had a hard time getting before they could play. Get a job. Or they.

And uh. Make them work. Today Bill, uh. The guys have more chance. Of learning the instruments than we had when we started. Because nothing myself. I'd have to pay for nothing. But the most musicians that time had to pay for their lessons. And now these guys come on your job and learn you for nothing. You know.
That's true. I've heard in the old days that say if a trumpet player went on the job and he wasn't so good they'd send him home before the night was over. Yeah.
Is that really true? That's true.
Yeah. Did you ever play in a band where anybody sent somebody home that way or? Well. Is that before your time you think?
Well that maybe before my time Bill. I have never had that uh.
I'm not trying to insult you but nobody ever send you home I guess in those days.
Well no. They could have Bill. Cause I wasn't good at all. I wasn't good at that management all the time.
But nobody on the job ever.
Never sent me home yet.
Or sent anybody else home that you remember when they were on the job?
No Bill no.
Did you hear about that?

Bill yes Bill I like to say that Bill. I like to say that because it sounded funny but I have sent a man home. You have done that haven't you? Yeah I have sent a man home. I have sent a sousaphone player home out of my band. See both of them showed up and the one would play the best I've kept. Oh yeah. And I sent the older man home. That made hard feelings.

Yeah. Do you remember you hear about the old dances too where they'd hire two bands like some of the society people maybe for a party I've heard of that. They have two bands there and they both play a few numbers and then they'll send one of them home pretty soon.

What band they like the best. What band the people likes the best they keep. Did they do that quite often they think? Well a lot of times it had been done. And then one time ago maybe Albert Walter will tell you the same thing I don't know if you remember. Every Monday we had things they call a banquet.
Oh yeah.
On Mondays. All the society, the many societies had banquets in high bands and had a lot to eat and a lot to drink.
Would that be in a home or some big hall?
No it was a big hall and all these big halls. Big halls of that.
Yeah all these big halls. Was that mostly for eating or for dancing or what was the main thing?
Well it was mostly for eating for society you know give the members eating and drinking and people dancing. A lot of people invited to come over and dance and have a nice time.
Do you remember some of the early dances like that? The bands that played some of those, do they call them sort of like banquets or how do they say some people call them banquets?
Banquets yeah banquets. We call them banquets. We used to call them banquets. But right there was banquets. Yeah. Yeah we used to call them banquets. Old Albert Glen every Monday we had one to play.
Yeah. Do you remember some of the bands that played those jobs? Some of the musicians you heard when you were young?

Oh yes. Yes. I remember a lot of those bands. They were old Jack Carey. I forgot to mention Jack my old friend. I did play with Jack Carey a couple of months before he taken sick and died. I played banquets with him. I played banquets with Buddy Petit. I played with Chris Kelly. Also with Kid René. Bill I played most every band in the city. Knowing band in the city. I really did. Played most every knowing band in the city. And good band.
Who were some of your favorite guitar and banjo players? Aside from your brother we know you must have thought John especially was wonderful everyone says.
Well everybody gave him that you know but not me I wouldn't brag about him.
I know you did.
But everybody gave him that.
So we know that he was great. And who were some of the others that you liked when you were a kid?

Well mostly fell there was a lot of guitar players like Willie San Diego. You know Mr. Willie San Diego. Also Mr. Lloyd Kepper. I know your name is Lloyd Kepper. Oh yes. Mr. Lloyd Kepper. A lot of other people I can't think about the name.
What about this fella Payne that you mentioned? Richard Payne. Was he really good?
Well I couldn't tell how good he was because I was too small. To remember he's called, you know he's playing when he was my dad and him. That's around 1910. About 10 years old.
You remember some of the fellas uptown like Brock Mumford. Brock who used to play with the Eagle Band.

No. Lorenzo Stoll. Oh Lorenzo Stoll. Yes I know him good. He was a nice musician too. Nice banjo player he was. He was a big banjo player. He was nice too. Also Willie Bonte. Oh yes. I forgot to mention his name. Willie Bonte was a nice guy too. Wonderful banjo player too. Remember Tom Benton.
Tom Benton yes.
Also him. I remember him.
Did he play banjo, guitar, mandolin or what did he do? Banjo.

But see Bill, when you called asked me this question then it comes to my remembrance. Yeah. But it's been so long I can't think about those girls guys. Sure. Yeah but really I know all them guys well. That was in my time.
I wonder if you can tell us about you say you started on guitar and then later switched to banjo. When you were a kid say ten years old were most of the bands using guitars or banjos?
They were using guitars Bill.
Most of them or all of them you think?
All of them I've seen they were using guitars that time. That would be 1910 about. That's around 1910 they were all using guitars.
You know before that if they'd ever used banjo did your father or Simon or John ever say?
No Bill. It was a long time, long time after that. It was around 1915. Tomorrow remember that banjo did get popular.
Maybe 1915. Something around the time.
Tomorrow remember that banjo did get popular.
Do you think John switched over about that time too? Do you know when you might have done it?
Yes, John switched over about that time too. From guitar to banjo.
He'd been playing guitar before then? He did play guitar yeah. And you switched then by 1917 your first job there along in there was on banjo. On banjo yeah.
I always loved my banjo.
But that time were almost all the bands using banjo or something else?

Oh yeah they were popular. You know banjo was a big thing in this town one time. If you couldn't play banjo they wouldn't hire you. The guitar was gone all just like the bass violins. Everybody switched then? Everybody switched. They switched the bass violins then the sousaphone come in style. They switched the sousaphone. The bass violins couldn't play the sousaphone he couldn't have no job.

Your father though never played sousaphone. No he never did. He died 1917. Around that time yeah Bill. But that time tubas weren't popular. No no no no. Which do you like best really? Banjo or guitar?

Bill I like the banjo not because I'm not much of a guitar player but I like the banjo for one reason. I think the banjo has more support to my own kind of music, jazz. It's more support to the band. More swinging. Yeah it's got a good drive.
You can hear it right.

I mean good drive. If you play it right and don't try to do too much. I mean it sounds good. Play with the fellas and compliment, give them the right compliment and the right chords. It sounds better. What I want to say Bill, when I was playing guitar it was different than now. Because the guys playing guitar now I never make a guitar player. Because a guitar is too hard now. You see all sorts of things as 13 chords. Yeah all those. And 10 and 9. We didn't have all those things. We didn't have all those different kind of chords. That's just added on to my feelings.
Did you ever hear John, your brother John say anything if he liked guitar better than banjo? Or which one he liked best or thought was best in the band?

Well I think John liked the banjo. Yeah cause he made more hit with the banjo. Good guitar player but he got more popular with the banjo. When banjo come out he got more popular. And he had a lot of scholars white and colored. Girls and boys.
When did he leave for New York? How long was he here?
Well John left for New York. Let me see. I live in that street.
Has he been up there 10 years or 2 or 3 years before he died?

Oh yeah been up there long before he died. Long time. Yeah he didn't, he didn't, John was up there he couldn't make it down here for my brother's funeral. Yeah he been in a good world before, 3 years before he died.
Well do you know, when did he go with Pierron? He was in one picture I have he's playing with Arlen Pierron's band.
He was, also Salmon was with Pierron too.

You didn't know that did you? I don't remember, usually John Lindsay was playing bass or somebody else, he was playing combo too. Yeah yeah. I saw John's picture with Pierron, he didn't go to New York with Pierron did he? No. Early in the 20's to make it.
But he went to New York with King Joe Oliver.
Oh he was up there with Oliver.
Him and Paul Bones too. Yeah.
At that time about 1929 or something like that. Yeah.
Yeah.

Just another minute or two on here, some of the bands that you played with you mentioned all these great trumpet players like Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly and Kid Rene, who was your favorite trumpet player in those days? Or Cornette, whatever they played.

Well uh, what was Cornette, that time Bill, Rene was the most jazzed man we had. I mean for fingering his corner and making those notes. And Sam Morgan was one of the sweetest trumpet players we had. But Chris Kelly, he had the ragged, ragged music you know, all the ragged music that people liked. The low class of people you know. Well he was king of that. I see many times we'd meet on the corner. Buddy Petit, Kid Rene, and Chris Kelly. We'd meet also Punch. Butch Miller, he was here, could tell you the same thing. They'd meet on the corner, George Boyd playing clarinet then. They'd meet on the corner. George Boyd playing clarinet there. And they'd meet on the corner. And stuff like

And they get there, at that time they didn't have trouble, they had news and where. They get together, they stay there. Stay there and play, watch Chiron Manila. Rene used to give a sign to go ahead, because Rene and Chris Keller's good friends, you see, he'd give Chris Keller a sign to go ahead and leave him to it. Chris would pull off, you see. And just leave Rene to handle that fella, because Rene could handle him. There was too much for Chris. We had a wonderful time, Bill. Show us some time whenever I was here now.
I'd like to hear that.

We didn't make much money, but we would be made, we'd done more with the money we made than we do with the money we make now. And then we had more work. The people I know, they respect us more, treat us more better.
Yeah, the musicians were popular then, I guess. Oh, Bill, you're talking about popular, Bill.
Bill, I have 611 children.
Oh yes, I'm trying to ask them about your children.

Yeah, I have 611 children and my wife. And then none of my children take music. None of them? Well... They wouldn't take it up. Not try it, my best. I got a drum there, guitar there. They got a bass violin there for them.
It's not too good a profession now, anyway.
They don't take it up. They don't see nothing in it, you know? Yeah.
Well, I guess they all like music though, I bet. Oh, they love it.
They really love it. They really love it. They love to hit play it.
Well, there's one other question, sort of a personal question. Some people have told about how you used to be a boxer and all. Did you really do any fighting professionally? No, Bill, no.

I never was no professional fighter there. That got out somehow or another. But I was a boxer, Bill. I was no fighter. I used to go around and box around the north side. That time, Lopo St. Roman. That time when Tico and them guys was coming up like that, you know? Before getting in the ring and fighting for real money. I never was that. I never could make that.
How heavy were you in those days?
Oh, Bill, I was about 125 pounds. That's pretty light. Yeah. But when was that? What period of your life?
How old were you? Oh, Bill.
I was about 21 years old in the day.
Cool stuff

segments.title: Birthplace and father William Marrero
segments.summary: Marrero gives his birth date and the Seventh Ward neighborhood, and his father's name and death around 1917 at age 47.

segments.title: Father's early band with Richard Payne and Big Eye Louie
segments.summary: He recalls his father's band, with Payne on guitar, Big Eye Louie on clarinet, called Imperial or Superior; his father was manager rather than leader.

segments.title: Father's instruments, not reading music, and bands he played in
segments.summary: His father played bass violin and guitar, never read music, and played with Freddie Keppard and a cornetist; brother John was Lawrence's first teacher.

segments.title: Mother's guitar playing and family string sessions
segments.summary: His mother sang and played guitar well; the family played string instruments together at home, starting with Under the Double Eagle.

segments.title: Learning by ear from John; Barnes and Frazier cousins
segments.summary: John taught him by ear; he explains how he is first cousin to Emile and Paul Barnes and to Josiah Frazier through the Frazier sisters.

segments.title: Brother Simon's brass band playing and the Frazier relatives
segments.summary: Simon played bass drum and sousaphone in brass bands, and Lawrence followed him; an uncle was a piano tuner and a cousin a piano player.

segments.title: Number of brothers and John's death in New York
segments.summary: Five brothers and two sisters, their birth order, and John's death in New York around 1940-41.

segments.title: Playing with Sam Morgan, Buddy Petit and Chris Kelly
segments.summary: He recalls his brothers in Morgan's and Petit's bands, his own trips with them, and regular membership in Chris Kelly's band.

segments.title: John Marrero's instruments, his wife, and self-teaching
segments.summary: John played banjo, guitar and piano, taught himself under their father; his widow could tell more about him.

segments.title: Simon on bass, father teaching the sons, first guitar
segments.summary: Their father taught all the sons; Simon became the bass player; Lawrence's first instrument was a six-string guitar shown by John.

segments.title: Spelling of his name and the Marrero surname
segments.summary: He spells his name, gives his middle name Henry, and hesitates over how his father got the Marrero name.

segments.title: Starting on six-string banjo and first jobs at seventeen
segments.summary: He began early on a banjo tuned like a guitar, subbed for John in Sam Morgan's and Celestin's bands, and was working at 17.

segments.title: Father practicing at home and his bowed bass
segments.summary: His father practiced at home, was a good chord man who bowed the bass and could be heard from afar.

segments.title: Old-time musicians versus today's
segments.summary: He says the music is going backward; the older players cared more, while today's learn for free.

segments.title: Musicians being sent home from a job
segments.summary: He was never sent home but once sent an older sousaphone player home from his own band, causing hard feelings.

segments.title: Monday banquets and bands he played with
segments.summary: Society banquets in big halls each Monday; he played them with Jack Carey, Buddy Petit, Chris Kelly and others.

segments.title: Favorite guitar and banjo players of his youth
segments.summary: He names Willie San Diego, Lloyd Keppard, Lorenzo Stoll, Willie Bonte and Tom Benton, and says his brother John was praised by everyone.

segments.title: Switch from guitar to banjo and banjo versus guitar
segments.summary: Guitars were universal around 1910, banjo took over about 1915, and he prefers banjo for its drive; chords are more complex today.

segments.title: John's banjo fame, move to New York and Oliver
segments.summary: John became popular on banjo with many students, appeared in Pierron's band, and went to New York with King Oliver and Paul Barnes.

segments.title: Favorite trumpeters: Rene, Morgan and Chris Kelly on the corner
segments.summary: He compares Kid Rene, Sam Morgan and Chris Kelly, and describes bands meeting on the corner and Rene handling rivals.

segments.title: His children and music
segments.summary: His children took no interest in playing, though they love music.

segments.title: Boxing in his youth
segments.summary: He was an amateur boxer at about 125 pounds around age 21, never a professional.
